items_missed: The move date was never asked. Not once in seven and a half minutes, on a call whose entire purpose is scheduling. She collected two full addresses, square footage, bedroom counts, garage use, walk distances at both ends, access concerns at both ends, box count, and packing scope — and never established when this family is moving. Availability was therefore never checked either. That is the single largest gap on a scheduler call: the walkthrough is now booked and the thing the walkthrough exists to price still has no date attached to it.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or any warm-up. 'Is it a convenient time to talk?' is a permission ask, not a warm-up, and it came before the customer had said a word.

Storage stops never asked. On a five-bedroom, 2,227 sq ft house moving into a 1,557 sq ft three-bedroom townhome — a 30% reduction in space — an offsite storage unit is close to a default assumption, and it was never raised.

The moving-stressor question was never asked, and the customer supplied the stressor anyway — twice — and it was talked past both times. He said 'What happens if it's not, like it was more?' and then, more pointedly, 'What I'm saying is I don't know and there's no way for me to know. So when you guys show up, when you start packing and ends up being like a couple of boxes more or whatever, I don't know. You know what happens.' That is a customer telling a mover he is afraid of an open-ended bill. Roselyn's answer was 'Yeah. Okay. So for packing, you've also requested for packing.' She changed the subject. The whole reason to run a virtual walkthrough is to answer that exact fear, and she never said so.

The box-count question was asked in a way that could not produce a usable answer. 'Typical box count for your home size is 115 to 135 boxes. Do you feel that you fall within that range?' asks a customer who has not packed anything to validate a number he has no basis to evaluate — and he said as much. On a full-house packing job the box count drives both truck count and pack hours, and it is still unresolved.

'Normally, it will double the cost for packing and moving' was delivered as a bare fact with no framing, no number, and no value attached. It is accurate and it is the most expensive sentence on the call, and it landed on a customer who had just said he was worried about cost drift. It needed the other half: what the packing service actually buys him, and that the walkthrough will replace 'double' with a real figure.

No differentiator was mentioned at any point — not No Worries Damage Coverage, not Meet Your Mover, not the On-Time Guarantee, not no-hidden-fees, not no-deposit. Sections 3 through 7 are auto-credited under the walkthrough-scheduler rule, so this costs nothing on the score, but it is a real gap on the call: a full-house pack-and-move is the highest-anxiety job Einstein sells, and No Worries coverage was the obvious answer to the worry he actually voiced.

The walkthrough handoff was left dangling on the wife's availability with no owner and no time. The customer offered to bring her on immediately ('Actually, my wife could do it right now'), then asked twice how to proceed — 'do I call you back or she calls you back?' — and the answer was conditional and open-ended: 'I have already sent her the link, if she's not there then I'll call you back or I can also call her back in case.' No time was set, no fallback slot was booked, and the call ended with 'Just let her know. Thank you.' The link is out but nothing is actually scheduled.

Mika's name was captured phonetically and never confirmed — 'Mika MEK' — and the wife's number was read back as digits without a verification read-back, on a call where the sole deliverable is a link sent to that number.

Customer's name used once, in the greeting, and never confirmed. The call opened 'Hello Miguel! This is in from Einstein moving' against a caller ID that shows only a phone number, so the identity was assumed from the lead record and never verified with the person on the line.

Clarity was a live problem, not a transcription artifact in every case. 'In order for us to give you a perfect code' (quote), 'access concerns like narrow paths and hallways, steep drivers and pay walkway,' 'do we have access concerns by any chance? Like narrow batteries?' and 'do you think that's about $30, I mean, do you think it's about two-to-three school buses' are four separate places where the phrasing would be hard to parse live. The customer's isolated 'Hello.' early in the call reads like he was checking whether the line was working.
No rapport moment anywhere. Seven and a half minutes, no affirmation beyond 'okay' and 'no worries,' no acknowledgment of anything the customer said as a person rather than as a data point.
top_strength: Roselyn made the right structural call fast and she did not waste the customer's time getting there. A 2,227 sq ft five-bedroom house with a full-house packing request is squarely walkthrough territory, and rather than guessing at a number she said so plainly and asked for the appointment in the same breath: 'based on your home size normally, we do a virtual walkthrough in that way, we would just base it on the items that we're moving. Do you have time to complete the virtual walkthrough today?' Not 'would you be open to' — 'do you have time today.' When the customer said not right now but yes, she immediately went for a slot ('What time are you, or day are you available? Are you available on Tuesday, Wednesday?'), and when he countered with 'I'm available in like thirty minutes' she took it without friction. Then he offered his wife instead and Roselyn adapted in real time — got Mika's separate number, sent the link while still on the phone, and confirmed it was out: 'I have already sent her the link for the virtual walkthrough.' From 'do you have time today' to a link delivered took under two minutes. Her front-half data collection was also efficient and better sequenced than most. She recapped the quote form rather than re-asking it — address, square footage, story count — and then layered the questions that the form does not capture, at both ends, in the same order: garage use ('Can you still park your car inside the garage or this is only used for storage?'), walk distance from truck to front door, and access concerns. Asking the garage question that way is smart; 'do you park in it' is a far better proxy for how much is in there than 'do you have a garage.' She also caught and corrected the destination bedroom count mid-recitation rather than letting a form error ride, and she was honest about a hard constraint most reps would soften: 'a 26 foot box truck can only fit 100 boxes' and 'normally, it will double the cost for packing and moving.' Telling a customer the truck has a ceiling before he books is the kind of disclosure that prevents a move-day problem.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is a process gap rather than a skill gap: nothing on this call is actually scheduled. No move date was ever asked for, and the walkthrough ended with a link sent to a third party and no confirmed time — 'if she's not there then I'll call you back or I can also call her back in case.' The customer asked twice who calls whom and never got an answer he could act on. A scheduler call has to end with two things on the calendar. The close it needed: 'Perfect — give Mika a call now and I'll stay available for the next thirty minutes. If I haven't heard from either of you by 2:00, I'll call her directly. And before you go, what date are you targeting for the move itself? I want to see what we have open so we can hold it while we finish the estimate.' That is fifteen seconds and it converts a hopeful handoff into two commitments. Second priority, and this is the coaching that matters most: the customer told her what he was afraid of and she changed the subject. 'There's no way for me to know. So when you guys show up, when you start packing and ends up being a couple of boxes more or whatever, I don't know, you know what happens' is a customer asking whether this bill can run away from him. He said it after she had just told him packing would 'double the cost.' The answer was sitting right there and it is the entire reason the walkthrough exists: 'That is exactly why we do the walkthrough, sir — instead of guessing at 115 boxes, we look at the actual rooms together and I build the estimate off what is really there. And you are never charged for boxes you did not use; we bill for time and materials actually used, not for the guess. That is also what our No Worries Damage Coverage is for, and it is included.' Practice pairing every stated worry with the mechanism that answers it. Third: use the name, and verify it. 'Miguel' appears once, in the opening line, against a caller ID that shows only a number — it came off the lead record and was never confirmed with the person speaking. The wife's name was captured as 'Mika MEK' with no read-back, on a call whose only deliverable is a link to her phone. Read numbers and names back once, slowly, every time they are the thing the next step depends on. Fourth: pace and enunciation. Several phrases here would have been genuinely hard to follow live — 'a perfect code' for quote, 'narrow batteries' for narrow hallways, 'steep drivers and pay walkway.' This is worth pairing with the CET clarity coaching rather than treating as a one-off. Estimate-accuracy note, even though no estimate was quoted: the one input she did try to establish — the box count — is still unresolved, and she took a soft 'yes' to a range the customer openly said he could not evaluate. On a full-house pack that number drives pack hours, materials, and whether one 26-foot truck is enough for a five-bedroom home going into a townhome 30% smaller. Put 'count the boxes and walk the garage and any storage unit' on the walkthrough agenda explicitly, because the virtual tour will not surface a storage unit nobody asked about.
phone_presence_notes: Efficient but almost entirely transactional — no warm-up, no affirmations beyond 'okay' and 'no worries,' the customer's name used once and never confirmed, and the one emotional moment on the call (his repeated worry about not knowing his own box count) was answered by moving to the next form field; the customer's tone audibly sharpens on 'No. What I'm saying is I don't know and there's no way for me to know,' and it was not acknowledged.
audio_review_reason: Score of 2 triggers the low-warmth verification rule, and this call needs it more than most: the transcript may be understating her. Multiple phrases come through mangled in ways that could be either delivery or ASR ('a perfect code' for quote, 'narrow Paff and hallways,' 'Deep drivers and pay walkway,' 'narrow batteries,' '23 school buses'), and the customer's isolated 'Hello.' early on suggests a possible line or clarity issue rather than a flat delivery. Audio is needed to separate a genuine warmth-and-enunciation problem from a bad transcript before this is used to coach a CET rep.
